paras: The police beating of Leon Hunt occurred in Baltimore's Northwestern police section shortly before May 2, 1919, when officers answering a street fight reportedly shot a man in the leg and clubbed Hunt and Percy Stimenee. The Baltimore Afro-American presented it as an example of police beating Black residents for minor offenses.

According to residents quoted by the Afro-American, officers in the section had used their guns and clubs "freely on both men and women" since a policeman was shot while making an arrest some time earlier. Residents also complained that people taken to the station house had been beaten over the head until they lay senseless on the floor.

In the account of Hunt's friends, he tried to stop a fight between a man named Goodman and Robert Norris, 27, in front of 520 Gold street. When police arrived, everyone ran, and an officer is said to have fired "without further provocation," wounding a man in the left leg; the garbled text suggests it was Hunt. Friends alleged that after he fell, officers set upon Hunt and beat him over the head. Hunt and Stimenee, 23, were both treated for head wounds from police clubs.

Hunt, Elsworth Coates, 17, Sterling Rozer, 17, and Joshua Moses, 45, were charged in connection with the disturbance. All but Hunt were let off with slight fines, while Hunt put up $900 bail and asked to have his case sent to court. To stop what the paper called "unwarranted shooting and clashing" [clubbing], an attorney was engaged to carry the case to court and, ultimately, to the Police Board. No report of the outcome of Hunt's case or of any Police Board action appears in the coverage.

The only known report is a city-news story on page 2 of the Baltimore Afro-American of May 2, 1919. The paper opened not with the fight but with "the common practice of police in the Northwestern section of beating up colored people for slight infractions of the law," presenting Hunt's case as one instance of it. It relied on the version of Hunt's friends and neighborhood residents, gave no account from the police, and named none of the officers.
